title: Words and Prefixes in a Trie

concept.title: A tree of letters
body: A **trie** (prefix tree) stores a set of words in a tree where every edge is labelled with a letter. The words that share a beginning share the first part of their road: `car`, `cart` and `cat` all start with the road `c - a`. A node can be marked "a word ends here". Looking up a word or a prefix takes one step per letter, whatever the number of stored words.

The difference between the two queries is the end mark: `ca` is a **prefix** of `car`, but not a stored **word** unless it was inserted itself. Python dictionaries are a simple way to write a trie; in C++ and Java a node usually has an array of 26 children.

statement: Store `n` words in a set. Then answer `q` queries. A query `word s` asks whether `s` is exactly one of the stored words. A query `prefix s` asks whether at least one stored word starts with `s` (a word starts with itself). Print `yes` or `no` for every query.
inputFormat: The second line has the `n` words that are stored.
Each of the next `q` lines has a kind of query and a string: `word s` asks whether `s` is one of the stored words, `prefix s` asks whether some stored word starts with `s`.
constraints: Every word and every query string has 1 to 20 lowercase letters.

examples.input:
3
car cart cat
4
word car
word ca
prefix ca
prefix cx
examples.note: car is stored; ca is not a word but it is a prefix; cx is neither.

hints: Build a tree with one edge per letter; mark the node where a word ends.
For a query, follow the letters; if an edge is missing, the answer is no.
A word query also needs the end mark; a prefix query does not.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
words = input().split()
q = int(input())
queries = [input().split() for _ in range(q)]

# Your code here

explanation: Each word is inserted letter by letter, creating missing edges and marking its last node. A query follows its letters from the root: a missing edge means no; a word query also needs the end mark.
solution.complexity: Time O(total length of words and queries), space O(total length of words).
